summary:
North Dakota stands under the United States national framework in every respect that governs a trans visitor's documents, screening and entry. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, issues new passports only as M or F according to supporting documents, and leaves previously issued X-marker passports valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed those passport restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at processing, with some left stranded abroad.

Entry screening carries its own exposure. On 5 February 2025 an executive order titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" was issued, and on 25 February 2025 the State Department announced it would bar trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating as fraud, with a permanent bar, any applicant listing a gender other than the one assigned at birth. The Transportation Security Administration's checkpoint procedures involve secondary screening, hand-held devices and pat-downs that can be invasive of privacy and risk outing a trans traveller.

Within North Dakota itself, the legislative record is among the most restrictive for transgender adults. Erin Reed's July 2026 anti-trans legal-risk assessment map, built from five years of daily legislative tracking, lists North Dakota among "the worst states" for legislation targeting transgender adults and among the states that prohibit any changes to birth certificates, forcing trans people to out themselves when showing documents.

North Dakota's 2023 law bans all gender marker changes on birth certificates with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery, a stricter and more explicit surgical requirement than in many other states; the Movement Advancement Project marks North Dakota a "negative law" state on its identity-document tracker. Accompanying regulations to the May 2023 bill were rejected, leaving in place a 2008 regulation restricting changes to those who have undergone a sex conversion operation. By contrast, the North Dakota Department of Transportation updates driver licence and state ID gender markers upon receipt of a physician or therapist letter stating the applicant completed a permanent gender role transition.

Facilities and schools are also regulated. An April 2023 law, signed by the Governor and effective 1 July 2023, explicitly allows restriction of transgender individuals' public bathroom usage in many state-run facilities. House Bill 1522 (2023), an act creating new sections of the North Dakota Century Code relating to preferred pronouns and providing accommodations to a transgender student, carries a penalty provision and an emergency clause; it was signed by the governor with the last official action filed with the Secretary of State on 9 May 2023. A May 2023 law effective 1 July forbids schools and government entities from requiring or prohibiting preferred pronoun use but requires disclosure and outing of transgender students to parents in state-run schools.

Providing gender-affirming care to minors is illegal under a North Dakota bill passed by a veto-proof majority on 5 April 2023. Transgender girls were targeted by 2021 legislation banning participation in girls' school sports teams, passed 69 to 25 in the House and 27 to 20 in the Senate and vetoed by Governor Doug Burgum on 21 April 2021, followed in April 2023 by two bills signed into law banning individuals assigned male at birth from female sports and athletics in schools and higher education respectively.

Discrimination protections are thin. North Dakota statutes do not explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of gender identity, though Bostock v. Clayton County (15 June 2020) established that Title VII protects employees from workplace discrimination on the basis of gender identity. Limited city-level protections exist in Grand Forks for city employees and applicants and in rental housing from 2013. An April 2021 state law allows student groups at colleges, universities and high schools to discriminate against LGBT students. State hate crime law does not cover gender identity, though federal law since the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act allows federal prosecution for crimes based on gender identity. A June 2021 committee regulation bans conversion therapy by social workers, psychologists and counselors.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 26 June 2015 under Obergefell v. Hodges, and adoption by individuals is permitted with no express ban on LGBTQ people or same-sex couples, though state law expressly allows private adoption agencies to discriminate based on sincerely held religious belief. A 2022 Public Religion Research Institute poll found 78 percent of residents supported an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity while 22 percent were opposed.
tangentialFactors:
North Dakota's trajectory mirrors a wider national pattern documented by rights trackers: state legislatures closing birth-certificate gender-marker changes, restricting facilities access, and banning gender-affirming care for minors. Kansas enacted a comparable law in March 2026 invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not match sex assigned at birth, which rights groups describe as a template for other state legislatures. Nationally, state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and, in some states, government buildings cover 9 states and 1 territory, while 29 states, 4 territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states.

In July 2020 North Dakota Republican delegates voted for the party's 2020 election platform opposing absolutely any civil rights protections for LGBTQ people while accusing transgender people "of preying on women" and LGBTQ people of "recruiting children". Many Republican delegates condemned the platform, and Governor Doug Burgum opposed it as "divisive and divisional," stating "As I've long said, all North Dakotans deserve to be treated equally and live free of discrimination."

Perceptions toward gender and sexuality within Native American tribes in North Dakota differ from those of people of European descent, with traditions of "third gender" people also called "two-spirit" who perform tasks and wear clothes considered gender non-conforming, identified as skuxát among the Arikara, miati and mihdeke among the Hidatsa and Mandan, and wįktą, winkta and wíŋkte among the Assiniboine, Dakota and Lakota.

The federal measures in force or in litigation that bear on a trans visitor to North Dakota include Executive Order 14168, the passport sex-marker restrictions, the February 2025 trans-athlete visa bar, Executive Order 14187 on gender-affirming care for minors, and the military purge under Executive Order 14183. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position on any given measure should be checked before travel.

An April 2021 law allows student groups at colleges, universities and high schools to discriminate against LGBT students, and a March 2023 bill passed to allow businesses to refuse service on any grounds based on religious objective alone awaited gubernatorial action. State hate crime law does not cover gender identity, though federal law since the 2009 Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act allows federal prosecution for crimes based on gender identity. A June 2021 committee regulation bans conversion therapy by social workers, psychologists and counselors.

Dalrymple suspended in January 2015 and the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians legalizing same-sex marriage on its reservation by 6 to 2 in August 2020. Adoption by individuals is permitted with no express ban on LGBTQ people or same-sex couples, though a 1980s Supreme Court ruling made parental sexual orientation decisive in custody because of societal prejudices before reversal in 2003, while state law expressly allows private adoption agencies to discriminate based on sincerely held religious belief. Lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilization with state law recognizing the non-genetic, non-gestational mother as legal parent after donor insemination irrespective of marital status, with gestational surrogacy expressly permitted for intended parents whether same-sex or different-sex and traditional surrogacy prohibited.

Private adult consensual homosexual relations were legalized in 1973 as part of a Criminal Code revision setting universal age of consent at eighteen. A 2022 Public Religion Research Institute poll found 78 percent of residents supported an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation and gender identity while 22 percent were opposed.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Movement Advancement Project tracker and the North Dakota Legislative Branch overview of HB 1522 describe the birth-certificate and pronoun statutes, but the inventory does not resolve whether the 2008 regulation restricting gender-marker changes to those who have undergone a sex conversion operation remains in force alongside the 2023 statute; this is unresolved on the present sources.

The inventory does not document any North Dakota-specific enforcement action against a trans visitor under the April 2023 bathroom-restriction law or the May 2023 pronoun-outing statute; the only documented arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law in the sources occurred in Florida in April 2025.

Whether the North Dakota Department of Transportation's policy of updating driver licence and state ID gender markers upon receipt of a physician or therapist letter has been altered by Executive Order 14168 or any subsequent state action is not sourced here.

The status of the March 2023 bill allowing businesses to refuse service on religious grounds is recorded as awaiting gubernatorial action; whether it was subsequently signed is not sourced.

Erin Reed's July 2026 map classifies North Dakota among "the worst states" for legislation targeting transgender adults, but the underlying rubric's specific scoring for North Dakota is not reproduced in the inventory.
